claim: Kap123 is a major karyopherin protein of budding yeast.
source: Kap123, a major karyopherin protein of budding yeast, recognizes the nuclear localization signals (NLSs) of cytoplasmic histones H3 and H4 and translocates them into the nucleus during DNA replication.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a characterization of Kap123.

claim: Kap123 recognizes the nuclear localization signals (NLSs) of cytoplasmic histones H3 and H4.
source: Kap123, a major karyopherin protein of budding yeast, recognizes the nuclear localization signals (NLSs) of cytoplasmic histones H3 and H4 and translocates them into the nucleus during DNA replication.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by crystal structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kap123 translocates histones H3 and H4 into the nucleus during DNA replication.
source: Kap123, a major karyopherin protein of budding yeast, recognizes the nuclear localization signals (NLSs) of cytoplasmic histones H3 and H4 and translocates them into the nucleus during DNA replication.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known function of Kap123.

claim: The crystal structure of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 alone was determined.
source: Here, we report crystal structures of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 alone and in complex with H3- and H4-NLSs.
evidence: Reported in the abstract and detailed in the Results section with crystallographic data.

claim: The crystal structure of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 in complex with H3-NLS was determined.
source: Here, we report crystal structures of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 alone and in complex with H3- and H4-NLSs.
evidence: Reported in the abstract and detailed in the Results section with crystallographic data.

claim: The crystal structure of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 in complex with H4-NLS was determined.
source: Here, we report crystal structures of full-length Kluyveromyces lactis Kap123 alone and in complex with H3- and H4-NLSs.
evidence: Reported in the abstract and detailed in the Results section with crystallographic data.

claim: Kap123 possesses two discrete lysine-binding pockets for NLS recognition.
source: Structures reveal the unique feature of Kap123 that possesses two discrete lysine-binding pockets for NLS recognition.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: H3- and H4-NLSs share at least one of two lysine-binding pockets in Kap123.
source: Structural comparison illustrates that H3- and H4-NLSs share at least one of two lysine-binding pockets, suggesting that H3- and H4-NLSs are mutually exclusive.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparison in the Results section.

claim: H3- and H4-NLSs are mutually exclusive with respect to Kap123 binding.
source: Structural comparison illustrates that H3- and H4-NLSs share at least one of two lysine-binding pockets, suggesting that H3- and H4-NLSs are mutually exclusive.
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison and supported by competition assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Acetylation of key lysine residues at NLS weakens the interaction with Kap123.
source: Additionally, acetylation of key lysine residues at NLS, particularly H4-NLS diacetylation, weakens the interaction with Kap123.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in Figure 5.

claim: H4-NLS diacetylation weakens the interaction with Kap123.
source: Additionally, acetylation of key lysine residues at NLS, particularly H4-NLS diacetylation, weakens the interaction with Kap123.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in Figure 5.

claim: Cytoplasmic histone H4 diacetylation weakens the Kap123-H4-NLS interaction thereby facilitating histone Kap123-H3-dependent H3:H4/Asf1 complex nuclear translocation.
source: These data support that cytoplasmic histone H4 diacetylation weakens the Kap123-H4-NLS interaction thereby facilitating histone Kap123-H3-dependent H3:H4/Asf1 complex nuclear translocation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: The nucleosome is the basic unit of eukaryotic chromatin.
source: The basic unit of eukaryotic chromatin is the nucleosome, where 146 base pairs of DNA wrap around a histone octamer composed of two copies of core histones H3, H4, H2A, and H2B (Luger et al., 1997; White et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 146 base pairs of DNA wrap around a histone octamer in the nucleosome.
source: The basic unit of eukaryotic chromatin is the nucleosome, where 146 base pairs of DNA wrap around a histone octamer composed of two copies of core histones H3, H4, H2A, and H2B (Luger et al., 1997; White et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The histone octamer is composed of two copies of core histones H3, H4, H2A, and H2B.
source: The basic unit of eukaryotic chromatin is the nucleosome, where 146 base pairs of DNA wrap around a histone octamer composed of two copies of core histones H3, H4, H2A, and H2B (Luger et al., 1997; White et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Each core histone contains an unstructured N-terminal tail that possesses NLSs.
source: Each core histone contains an unstructured N-terminal tail that possesses NLSs and several known sites for post-translational modifications (PTMs) including acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation (Strahl and Allis, 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Core histone N-terminal tails contain several known sites for post-translational modifications including acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation.
source: Each core histone contains an unstructured N-terminal tail that possesses NLSs and several known sites for post-translational modifications (PTMs) including acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation (Strahl and Allis, 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Histone tail chemical modifications play important roles in controlling DNA template-dependent processes.
source: These histone tail chemical modifications play important roles in controlling many DNA template-dependent processes, such as gene transcription, DNA replication, DNA repair, and histone deposition and nucleosome assembly (Strahl and Allis, 2000; Berger, 2002; Cosgrove and Wolberger, 2005; Jenuwein and Allis, 2001; Krebs, 2007; Marmorstein, 2001).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The entirety of the genomic DNA, including the number of nucleosomes, is duplicated during S phase.
source: The entirety of the genomic DNA, including the number of nucleosomes, is duplicated during S phase.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Pre-existing nucleosomes undergo disassembly and reassembly processes from one parental chromatid to one of two sister chromatids during DNA replication.
source: While DNA polymerases replicate the genomic DNA, pre-existing nucleosomes undergo disassembly and reassembly processes from one parental chromatid to one of two sister chromatids (Ransom et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Nascent histones are synthesized at the cytosol and imported into the nucleus to meet the demand for nucleosome shortage during S phase.
source: Meanwhile, the same amount of nascent histones are synthesized at the cytosol and imported into the nucleus to meet the demand for nucleosome shortage (Franco et al., 2005; Verreault, 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Asf1 is a H3/H4-specific histone chaperone.
source: Asf1, a H3/H4-specific histone chaperone, subsequently associates with the histones and forms a heterotrimeric H3:H4/Asf1 complex (Campos et al., 2010; Keck and Pemberton, 2012; Tyler et al., 1999; Natsume et al., 2007; English et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Asf1 associates with histones H3 and H4 and forms a heterotrimeric H3:H4/Asf1 complex.
source: Asf1, a H3/H4-specific histone chaperone, subsequently associates with the histones and forms a heterotrimeric H3:H4/Asf1 complex (Campos et al., 2010; Keck and Pemberton, 2012; Tyler et al., 1999; Natsume et al., 2007; English et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Asf1 shields histones H3 and H4 from undesired non-specific interactions.
source: Asf1 shields histones H3 and H4 from undesired non-specific interactions and safely delivers them into the nucleus for de novo nucleosome assembly.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a known function of Asf1.

claim: Asf1 safely delivers histones H3 and H4 into the nucleus for de novo nucleosome assembly.
source: Asf1 shields histones H3 and H4 from undesired non-specific interactions and safely delivers them into the nucleus for de novo nucleosome assembly.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as a known function of Asf1.

claim: Newly synthesized histones H3 and H4 are prone to be acetylated mainly at the N-terminal tail.
source: Soon after their synthesis, histones H3 and H4 are prone to be acetylated mainly at the N-terminal tail, where their NLSs are located.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The diacetylation of histone H4 at K5 and K12 is the most evolutionarily conserved PTM identified to date.
source: The most evolutionarily conserved PTM identified to date is the diacetylation of histone H4 at K5 and K12 (H4 K5ac and K12ac) (Sobel et al., 1994; Sobel et al., 1995; Loyola et al., 2006; Jasencakova et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Histone H4 K5 and K12 cytoplasmic diacetylation does not appear to be essential for cell survival.
source: Although highly conserved among eukaryotes, histone H4 K5 and K12 cytoplasmic diacetylation does not appear to be essential for cell survival (Ai and Parthun, 2004; Barman et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In fungi, histone H4 K5 and K12 diacetylation appears to be dispensable for nucleosome deposition.
source: Additionally, in fungi, the diacetylation appears to be dispensable for nucleosome deposition, suggesting a potential role in the nuclear translocation (Ma et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Macromolecules larger than 40 kDa cannot pass through the nuclear pore complex by simple diffusion.
source: Macromolecules larger than 40 kDa cannot pass through the nuclear pore complex by simple diffusion and require the assistance of active transporters called karyopherins (Kaps) (Stewart, 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Macromolecules larger than 40 kDa require the assistance of active transporters called karyopherins.
source: Macromolecules larger than 40 kDa cannot pass through the nuclear pore complex by simple diffusion and require the assistance of active transporters called karyopherins (Kaps) (Stewart, 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Kap proteins recognize either NLS or the nuclear export signal in order to import or export cargo proteins.
source: The family of Kap proteins recognizes either NLS or the nuclear export signal in order to import or export cargo proteins, respectively (Baake et al., 2001; Mühlhäusser et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nineteen human Kaps and fourteen budding yeast Kaps have been identified.
source: To date, nineteen human Kaps and fourteen budding yeast Kaps have been identified (Görlich and Kutay, 1999).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Eleven human and ten budding yeast Kaps mediate the import of cargo proteins to the nucleus.
source: Among them, eleven human and ten budding yeast Kaps are known to mediate the import of cargo proteins to the nucleus and the rest are responsible for either unidirectional export or the bidirectional import/export process of cargo proteins (Chook and Süel, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Kap proteins share the common structural motif of helical tandem HEAT repeats with a right-handed superhelical solenoid structure.
source: Kap proteins share the common structural motif of helical tandem HEAT (Huntingtin, elongation factor 3 (EF3), protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), and the yeast kinase TOR1) repeats with a right-handed superhelical solenoid structure (Stewart, 2007; Mosammaparast and Pemberton, 2004; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The NLS is a structurally disordered region of cargo proteins that is composed of overall positively charged residues with limited sequence homology.
source: The NLS is a structurally disordered region of cargo proteins that is composed of overall positively charged residues with limited sequence homology (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Kap proteins mostly recognize NLSs through their inner concave surface.
source: Kap proteins mostly recognize NLSs through their inner concave surface (Xu et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2006; Marfori et al., 2011; Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The lack of sequence conservation among NLSs allows a small number of Kap proteins to translocate a large number of nuclear proteins into the nucleus.
source: The lack of sequence conservation among NLSs allows a small number of Kap proteins to translocate a large number of nuclear proteins into the nucleus, which means that a single Kap protein can translocate many substrates (Chook and Süel, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: A single cargo protein can be imported via several Kap proteins.
source: Conversely, a single cargo protein can be imported via several Kap proteins.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Kap123 is the most abundant karyopherin in budding yeast.
source: Kap123, the most abundant karyopherin in budding yeast, functions as a primary transporter for the H3:H4/Asf1 complex, whereas Kap121 acts as a secondary transporter (Mosammaparast et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Kap123 functions as a primary transporter for the H3:H4/Asf1 complex.
source: Kap123, the most abundant karyopherin in budding yeast, functions as a primary transporter for the H3:H4/Asf1 complex, whereas Kap121 acts as a secondary transporter (Mosammaparast et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Kap121 acts as a secondary transporter for the H3:H4/Asf1 complex.
source: Kap123, the most abundant karyopherin in budding yeast, functions as a primary transporter for the H3:H4/Asf1 complex, whereas Kap121 acts as a secondary transporter (Mosammaparast et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citation.

claim: Residues 1–28 of histone H3 were designated as histone H3 NLS in budding yeast.
source: In budding yeast, residues 1–28 of histone H3 (H31–28-NLS) and residues 1–34 of histone H4 (H41–34-NLS) were respectively designated as histone H3 and H4 NLSs (Mosammaparast et al., 2002; Blackwell et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Residues 1–34 of histone H4 were designated as histone H4 NLS in budding yeast.
source: In budding yeast, residues 1–28 of histone H3 (H31–28-NLS) and residues 1–34 of histone H4 (H41–34-NLS) were respectively designated as histone H3 and H4 NLSs (Mosammaparast et al., 2002; Blackwell et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The crystal structure of full length Kl Kap123 was determined using the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) method.
source: The crystal structure of full length Kl Kap123 was determined using the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) method and refined at 2.35 Å resolution with a crystallographic R value of 20.99% and a free R value of 23.49% (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with crystallographic statistics.

claim: The crystal structure of full length Kl Kap123 was refined at 2.35 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure of full length Kl Kap123 was determined using the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) method and refined at 2.35 Å resolution with a crystallographic R value of 20.99% and a free R value of 23.49% (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with crystallographic statistics.

claim: Crystals of Kl Kap123 contain two copies of full-length Kl Kap123 per asymmetric unit.
source: Crystals contain two copies of full-length Kl Kap123 per asymmetric unit.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a crystallographic observation.

claim: The refined structure of Kl Kap123 displays 24 tandem HEAT repeats with a right-handed superhelical solenoid structure.
source: The refined structure displays 24 tandem HEAT repeats with a right-handed superhelical solenoid structure (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The first HEAT repeat (residues 1–39) of Kl Kap123 is disordered in the final structure.
source: The first HEAT repeat (residues 1–39), an intra-loop of repeat 8 (residues 325–329), repeat 15 (residues 631–656) and repeat 18 (residues 818–828) are disordered in the final structure (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: An intra-loop of repeat 8 (residues 325–329) of Kl Kap123 is disordered in the final structure.
source: The first HEAT repeat (residues 1–39), an intra-loop of repeat 8 (residues 325–329), repeat 15 (residues 631–656) and repeat 18 (residues 818–828) are disordered in the final structure (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: Repeat 15 (residues 631–656) of Kl Kap123 is disordered in the final structure.
source: The first HEAT repeat (residues 1–39), an intra-loop of repeat 8 (residues 325–329), repeat 15 (residues 631–656) and repeat 18 (residues 818–828) are disordered in the final structure (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: Repeat 18 (residues 818–828) of Kl Kap123 is disordered in the final structure.
source: The first HEAT repeat (residues 1–39), an intra-loop of repeat 8 (residues 325–329), repeat 15 (residues 631–656) and repeat 18 (residues 818–828) are disordered in the final structure (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: The overall architecture of Kl Kap123 is similar to other known karyopherin structures, excepting repeat 23.
source: The overall architecture of Kl Kap123 is similar to other known karyopherin structures (Xu et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2006; Marfori et al., 2011; Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013), excepting repeat 23 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citations and figures.

claim: The unique extra-long helix of repeat 23 is conserved in budding yeasts, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and K. lactis.
source: The unique extra-long helix of repeat 23 is conserved in budding yeasts, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and K. lactis, and establishes an intra-molecular interaction with repeats 12–14 using electrostatic and hydrogen bond interactions.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: The extra-long helix of repeat 23 establishes an intra-molecular interaction with repeats 12–14 using electrostatic and hydrogen bond interactions.
source: The unique extra-long helix of repeat 23 is conserved in budding yeasts, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and K. lactis, and establishes an intra-molecular interaction with repeats 12–14 using electrostatic and hydrogen bond interactions.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intra-molecular interaction of repeat 23 with repeats 12–14 may further stabilize the superhelical architecture of Kl Kap123.
source: This interaction may further stabilize the superhelical architecture of Kl Kap123 (Figure 1b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as an inference from structural data.

claim: The full-length Kl Kap123 crystal structure in the presence of histone H31–28 peptide was determined at 2.7 Å resolution.
source: To examine how Kap123 recognizes H3-NLS, we determined the full-length Kl Kap123 crystal structure in the presence of a histone H31–28 peptide (1–ARTKQTARKSTGGKA PRKQLASKAARK–28) at 2.7 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with crystallographic data.

claim: No major structural change of Kap123 was observed upon H3 peptide binding with Cα root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) of 0.4 Å.
source: No major structural change of Kap123 was observed upon the H3 peptide binding with Cα root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) of 0.4 Å.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural comparison.

claim: Only residues 12–17 and 21–26 of histone H3 were clearly visible in the Kap123-H31–28-NLS crystal structure.
source: Although we used the histone H31–28 peptide for crystallization, only residues 12–17 and 21–26 of histone H3 (12-GGKAPR-17 and 21-ASKAAR-26) were clearly visible, indicating that H3 peptide residues 1–11, 18–20 and 27–28 were disordered in the crystal structure and not critical for H3-NLS recognition by Kap123 (Figure 2a,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: H3 peptide residues 1–11, 18–20 and 27–28 were disordered in the Kap123-H31–28-NLS crystal structure.
source: Although we used the histone H31–28 peptide for crystallization, only residues 12–17 and 21–26 of histone H3 (12-GGKAPR-17 and 21-ASKAAR-26) were clearly visible, indicating that H3 peptide residues 1–11, 18–20 and 27–28 were disordered in the crystal structure and not critical for H3-NLS recognition by Kap123 (Figure 2a,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: H3 peptide residues 1–11, 18–20 and 27–28 are not critical for H3-NLS recognition by Kap123.
source: Although we used the histone H31–28 peptide for crystallization, only residues 12–17 and 21–26 of histone H3 (12-GGKAPR-17 and 21-ASKAAR-26) were clearly visible, indicating that H3 peptide residues 1–11, 18–20 and 27–28 were disordered in the crystal structure and not critical for H3-NLS recognition by Kap123 (Figure 2a,e).
evidence: Inferred from the disorder of these residues in the crystal structure.

claim: The H31–28-NLS peptide interacts with Kap123 through two deep lysine-binding pockets separately located at the Kap123 inner concave surface.
source: The determined structure revealed that the H31–28-NLS peptide interacts with Kap123 through two deep lysine-binding pockets separately located at the Kap123 inner concave surface (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The binding pattern of H31–28-NLS toward Kap123 is unique and clearly distinguishable from any known karyopherin-NLS structures.
source: The binding pattern of H31–28-NLS toward Kap123 is unique and clearly distinguishable from any known karyopherin-NLS structures (Xu et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2006; Marfori et al., 2011; Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: K14 and K23 of H31–28-NLS independently interact with two distinct and distal lysine-binding pockets of Kap123.
source: K14 and K23 of H31–28-NLS independently interact with two distinct and distal lysine-binding pockets, demonstrating that H31-28-NLS recognizes Kap123 in the bipartite binding mode (Figure 2b,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: H31-28-NLS recognizes Kap123 in the bipartite binding mode.
source: K14 and K23 of H31–28-NLS independently interact with two distinct and distal lysine-binding pockets, demonstrating that H31-28-NLS recognizes Kap123 in the bipartite binding mode (Figure 2b,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kap123 does not recognize the specific sequence of the middle region (residues 15–22) of H31–28-NLS.
source: Kap123 does not recognize the specific sequence of the middle region (residues 15–22) of H31–28-NLS (Figure 2b,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first lysine-binding pocket is organized through the inner surface residues of repeats 20–22 of Kap123.
source: The first lysine-binding pocket is organized through the inner surface residues of repeats 20–22 of Kap123 (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kap123 Y926 and the stretched aliphatic chain of H3 K14 form a hydrophobic interaction.
source: Kap123 Y926 (repeat 20) and the stretched aliphatic chain of H3 K14 form a hydrophobic interaction.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: The negatively charged pocket composed of N980, E1016, and E1017 and the positively charged ε-amine group of H3 K14 form several electrostatic and hydrogen bond interactions.
source: The negatively charged pocket composed of N980, E1016, and E1017 (repeats 21 and 22) and the positively charged ε-amine group of H3 K14 form several electrostatic and hydrogen bond interactions, which provide specificity toward H3 K14.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: The second lysine-binding pocket is established with repeats 11–13 of Kap123.
source: The second lysine-binding pocket is established with repeats 11–13 of Kap123 (Figure 2b,d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: H3 K23 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket through the hydrophobic interaction with F512.
source: H3 K23 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket through the hydrophobic interaction with F512 (repeat 12) as well as electrostatic interactions with D465 (repeat 11), S505, S509 (repeat 12), and N556 (repeat 13) in a similar manner as that of the first lysine-binding pocket.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: H3 K23 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket through electrostatic interactions with D465, S505, S509, and N556.
source: H3 K23 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket through the hydrophobic interaction with F512 (repeat 12) as well as electrostatic interactions with D465 (repeat 11), S505, S509 (repeat 12), and N556 (repeat 13) in a similar manner as that of the first lysine-binding pocket.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: Both Kap123 lysine-binding pockets produce a negatively charged groove to accommodate a lysine residue side chain.
source: Both Kap123 lysine-binding pockets produce a negatively charged groove to accommodate a lysine residue side chain.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a structural observation.

claim: The overall architecture of both lysine-binding pockets closely resembles the aromatic cage observed in the PHD finger domain, particularly similar to the H3K4me0 binding motif.
source: The overall architecture of both lysine-binding pockets closely resembles the aromatic cage observed in the PHD finger domain, particularly similar to the H3K4me0 binding motif (Sanchez and Zhou, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: Lysine residue acetylation abolishes electrostatic interactions thereby triggering H31–28-NLS dissociation from Kap123.
source: Lysine residue acetylation abolishes electrostatic interactions thereby triggering H31–28-NLS dissociation from Kap123.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as an inference from structural data.

claim: An acetylation mimic of K14 (K14Q), but not K9Q and K18Q, dramatically reduced GFP reporter nuclear localization.
source: A previous H3-NLS-GFP reporter assay demonstrated that an acetylation mimic of K14 (K14Q), but not K9Q and K18Q, dramatically reduced GFP reporter nuclear localization, which is in good agreement with our structure (Blackwell et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: The H3-NLS K14R mutation showed a minor effect with respect to nuclear localization.
source: The H3-NLS K14R mutation, which maintains the positive charge of the lysine side chain, showed a minor effect with respect to nuclear localization, indicating that the positive charge of Lys14 plays a key role in the nuclear translocation of H3-NLS mediated by Kap123 (Blackwell et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: The positive charge of Lys14 plays a key role in the nuclear translocation of H3-NLS mediated by Kap123.
source: The H3-NLS K14R mutation, which maintains the positive charge of the lysine side chain, showed a minor effect with respect to nuclear localization, indicating that the positive charge of Lys14 plays a key role in the nuclear translocation of H3-NLS mediated by Kap123 (Blackwell et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: Mutations of residues at the first lysine-binding pocket (Y926A, N980A, E1016A and E1017A) substantially reduced H31–28-NLS and Kap123 binding.
source: Mutations of residues at the first lysine-binding pocket (Y926A, N980A, E1016A and E1017A) and the second lysine-binding pocket (S505A and S509A) substantially reduced H31–28-NLS and Kap123 binding, indicating that the two lysine-binding pockets are indeed involved in H31–28-NLS recognition (Figure 3a,b,d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations of residues at the second lysine-binding pocket (S505A and S509A) substantially reduced H31–28-NLS and Kap123 binding.
source: Mutations of residues at the first lysine-binding pocket (Y926A, N980A, E1016A and E1017A) and the second lysine-binding pocket (S505A and S509A) substantially reduced H31–28-NLS and Kap123 binding, indicating that the two lysine-binding pockets are indeed involved in H31–28-NLS recognition (Figure 3a,b,d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations that interrupt the intra-molecular interaction between the extended helix of repeat 23 and residues at the ridge of repeats 12–14 of Kap123 almost abolished H31–28-NLS peptide binding.
source: Notably, mutations that interrupt the intra-molecular interaction between the extended helix of repeat 23 and residues at the ridge of repeats 12–14 of Kap123 almost abolished H31–28-NLS peptide binding (Figure 3c,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Kap123-H41–34-NLS complex co-crystal structure was determined at 2.82 Å resolution.
source: To investigate how Kap123 recognizes H4-NLS, we also determined the Kap123-H41–34-NLS complex co-crystal structure at 2.82 Å resolution using a H41–34 peptide for co-crystallization (1-SGRGKGGKGLGKGGAKRHRKILRDNIQGITKPAI-34) (Figure 4a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with crystallographic data.

claim: The Kap123-H41–34-NLS structure shows clear electron density for residues 13–20 of H41–34-NLS.
source: The Kap123-H41–34-NLS structure shows clear electron density for residues 13–20 of H41–34-NLS (13-GGAKRHRK-20) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H41–34-NLS K16 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket of Kap123 in a similar pattern to H31–28-NLS.
source: Notably, H41–34-NLS K16 binds to the second lysine-binding pocket of Kap123 in a similar pattern to H31–28-NLS (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The same residues that participate in H3 K23 recognition (S505, S509, F512 and N556) form the binding pocket to accommodate H4 K16.
